growth_story.headline: Malaysia's 1990s boom ended in the 1997-98 crisis; since 1998 income per person has grown 2.4 percent a year and now stands at a new high.
growth_story.arc: Income per person grew 6.4 percent a year from 1990 to 1997, as the strong performance the IMF describes continued through the 1990s. The 1997-98 Asian financial crisis ended that era: income per person fell 9.6 percent in 1998, and investment dropped from 43.1 to 26.8 percent of GDP. A quick rebound followed in 1999 and 2000, led by world demand for electronics, but growth has averaged 2.4 percent a year from 1998 to 2025, and an ADB study finds private investment never fully recovered from the crisis. Income per person fell again in 2009 and by 6.7 percent in 2020, then came back. Growth averaged 2.9 percent a year over 2006-2015 and 2.6 over 2016-2025, and income per person reached a new high in 2025.

threads.title: The 1997-98 crisis
threads.text: Malaysia grew fast through the 1990s until the Asian financial crisis. Growth turned sharply negative in early 1998, and the slump was worse than expected. The rebound in 1999 and 2000 was led by world demand for electronics.

threads.title: Investment never fully recovered
threads.text: Investment fell from 43.1 percent of GDP in 1997 to 26.8 in 1998 and has stayed far lower since. An ADB study found that private investment never fully recovered from the crisis, and it links the problem to distortions in the New Economic Policy and the influence of government-linked corporations.

threads.title: Electronics and the tech cycle
threads.text: Electronics is still central to growth. Demand for electrical and electronic goods lifted growth in 2024, and technology-related foreign investment stayed strong in 2025. The IMF now lists a possible end to the AI boom as a risk.

growth_story.tension: Recent sources describe investment momentum strengthening, but in the data investment was 21.3 percent of GDP in 2025. That is below the 25.5 of 2016 and about half the 43.1 of 1997, so the recent strength is a rise from a low level, not a return to pre-crisis levels.
